options.text: Because it cannot know how the application uses a query's result
Because the application always declares its premises explicitly
Because premises are stored in the transaction log
Because the database can infer application logic from the query

questions.explanation: The database cannot infer every application invariant from SQL results, so it conservatively treats overlapping read-write dependencies as potentially dangerous. That may abort executions that the application knows are harmless.

questions.question: Which read-write timings can create an SSI dependency?

options.text: A concurrent write may occur before or after the snapshot read
Detecting dirty reads and dirty writes, both before the commit
Detecting deadlocks and phantoms, both at commit time
Detecting lost updates and read skew, both after the commit

questions.explanation: The two cases are distinguished by whether the conflicting write precedes or follows the read.

questions.question: How does SSI resolve two transactions with dangerous mutual dependencies?

options.text: It records both dependencies and aborts a transaction as needed
Transaction 43 sees on_call = false and commits successfully
Transaction 42 aborts and 43 commits with no conflict
Both transactions abort immediately on the stale read

questions.explanation: Snapshot visibility alone would let both commits create write skew. SSI records the read-write dependencies without blocking. Once one side commits, allowing the other dependency to commit would form a nonserializable cycle, so the later commit is aborted.

questions.question: Why doesn't SSI abort transaction 43 the moment the stale read is detected? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If transaction 43 was a read-only transaction, it wouldn't need to be aborted, because there is no risk of write skew
At the time when transaction 43 makes its read, the database doesn't yet know whether that transaction is going to later perform a write
Transaction 42 may yet abort or may still be uncommitted at the time when transaction 43 is committed, so the read may turn out not to have been stale after all
Aborting the transaction early would violate the durability guarantee

questions.explanation: By avoiding unnecessary aborts, SSI preserves snapshot isolation's support for long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.

questions.question: When one transaction writes data that another transaction previously read, what mechanism does SSI borrow from 2PL, and how does SSI change its behavior?

options.text: Index-range locks that record reads without blocking other transactions
Predicate locks, which do block other transactions from writing
Table-level locks, held until the next garbage collection pass
Row locks, held only for the duration of the single statement

questions.explanation: SSI uses index-range markers resembling predicate locks to remember what transactions read. Writers consult those markers to record dependencies, but unlike 2PL they do not block the readers.

questions.question: What does an SSI writer do when it encounters prior read markers?

options.text: Records a dependency rather than blocking those readers
It must block until all readers have committed, exactly like a write lock
It must abort all readers immediately
It need do nothing; readers check at their own commit time

questions.explanation: The index entry records who read the range. A writer consults it and creates dependency metadata; readers and writers continue, and SSI decides at commit whether a dangerous dependency requires an abort.

questions.question: When two transactions each notify the other of a stale read, which one commits and why?

options.text: Each notifies the other; the first to commit succeeds, the second aborts
Both commit, since neither had committed when the notifications arrived
Both abort, since each of them notified the other of a stale read
Transaction 43 commits and transaction 42 is the one that aborts

questions.explanation: When mutual dependencies form a dangerous structure, SSI can allow the first transaction to commit and abort the later one once the conflict becomes definite. The application then retries the loser.

questions.question: What trade-off does SSI face when tracking read ranges?

options.text: Fine tracking costs resources; coarse tracking causes false aborts
The choice between optimistic and pessimistic locking; PostgreSQL uses 2PL theory
The number of snapshot versions retained; PostgreSQL uses garbage collection theory
The abort timeout; PostgreSQL uses queueing theory

questions.explanation: Tracking exact rows or predicates improves precision but increases bookkeeping. Coarser ranges are cheaper and more conservative. PostgreSQL uses dependency-graph results to recognize some executions that remain serializable despite an apparent conflict.

questions.question: When does SSI retain good performance?

options.text: While contention and retry-causing aborts remain manageable
SSI blocks like 2PL and is limited to one core like serial execution
SSI blocks readers but not writers, and scales to one machine
SSI has no abort rate constraint

questions.explanation: Readers and writers do not block each other, giving SSI steadier latency than 2PL. Conflict detection can scale across machines, but high contention creates abort and retry work; read-only snapshots can often proceed without aborting.

questions.question: What are transactions for?

options.text: An abstraction hiding concurrency problems and certain faults
Transactions are a locking mechanism for protecting shared data
Transactions are a durability guarantee for writes
Transactions are a performance optimization for batched writes

questions.explanation: Transactions convert many partial-failure and concurrency cases into a clean commit-or-abort outcome. Applications can often handle the abort with one whole-operation retry instead of repairing intermediate states.

questions.question: Which applications can most safely use weak or no multi-object transactions?

options.text: Those whose operations are independent or confined to one object
Only financial applications have any real need for transactions
All applications need transactions to exactly the same degree
Only applications distributed across machines need transactions

questions.explanation: The need depends on how operations interact, not whether the data is prestigious. When failures or concurrent actions can leave several objects inconsistent, transactions move difficult recovery and isolation logic into the database.

questions.question: What burden shifts to an application that lacks transactions?

options.text: Recovering partial writes and preserving cross-object invariants
Only concurrency problems arise; faults are handled by replication
Only hardware faults arise; concurrency is handled by the application
No inconsistency arises without them; transactions are purely a convenience

questions.explanation: Without an atomic boundary, one half of a multi-object update may succeed while another fails, and concurrent operations may interleave. A stored unread count can then disagree permanently with the messages it summarizes.
